claim: DNA methylation (DNAm) at specific cytosine-phosphate-guanine (CpG) sites has been found to be strongly correlated with chronological age.
source: DNA methylation (DNAm) at specific cytosine-phosphate-guanine (CpG) sites has been found to be strongly correlated with chronological age.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about the relationship between DNA methylation and chronological age.

claim: Observational evidence suggests that epigenetic age acceleration may be associated with an increased risk of mortality and age-related diseases, including cancer.
source: Observational evidence suggests that epigenetic age acceleration (i.e. when an individual's biological age is greater than their chronological age) may be associated with an increased risk of mortality and age-related diseases, including cancer (Fransquet et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Fransquet et al., 2019.

claim: Epigenetic clocks are heritable indicators of biological ageing derived from DNAm data.
source: Epigenetic clocks are heritable indicators of biological ageing derived from DNAm data.
evidence: This is a definitional statement about epigenetic clocks based on established scientific understanding.

claim: Each epigenetic clock is based on DNAm levels measured at a different set of CpG sites, which capture distinctive features of epigenetic ageing.
source: Each clock is based on DNAm levels measured at a different set of CpG sites, which capture distinctive features of epigenetic ageing (Liu et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Liu et al., 2020.

claim: HannumAge is trained on 71 age-related CpGs found in blood.
source: HannumAge is trained on 71 age-related CpGs found in blood (Hannum et al., 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hannum et al., 2013.

claim: Intrinsic HorvathAge is based on 353 age-related CpGs found in several human tissues and cell types, and is further adjusted for blood cell counts.
source: Intrinsic HorvathAge is based on 353 age-related CpGs found in several human tissues and cell types, and is further adjusted for blood cell counts (Horvath, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Horvath, 2013.

claim: PhenoAge incorporates data from 513 CpGs associated with mortality and nine clinical biomarkers.
source: PhenoAge incorporates data from 513 CpGs associated with mortality and nine clinical biomarkers (i.e. albumin, creatinine, serum glucose, C-reactive protein, lymphocyte percentage, mean corpuscular volume, red cell distribution width, alkaline phosphatase and leukocyte count) (Levine et al., 2018)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Levine et al., 2018.

claim: GrimAge includes data from 1,030 CpGs associated with smoking pack-years and seven plasma proteins.
source: GrimAge includes data from 1,030 CpGs associated with smoking pack-years and seven plasma proteins (i.e. cystatin C, leptin, tissue inhibitor metalloproteinases 1, adrenomedullin, beta-2-microglobulin, growth differentiation factor 15, and plasminogen activation inhibitor 1 (PAI-1)) (Lu et al., 2019a).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lu et al., 2019a.

claim: HannumAge and Intrinsic HorvathAge are better predictors of chronological age.
source: Due to differences in their composition, HannumAge and Intrinsic HorvathAge are better predictors of chronological age (Hannum et al., 2013; Horvath, 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hannum et al., 2013 and Horvath, 2013.

claim: PhenoAge and GrimAge stand out for their ability to predict health and lifespan.
source: while PhenoAge and GrimAge stand out for their ability to predict health and lifespan (Levine et al., 2018; Lu et al., 2019a; McCrory et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Levine et al., 2018, Lu et al., 2019a, and McCrory et al., 2021.

claim: Several studies suggest that HannumAge, Intrinsic HorvathAge, PhenoAge and GrimAge acceleration are associated with cancer risk.
source: Several studies suggest that HannumAge, Intrinsic HorvathAge, PhenoAge and GrimAge acceleration are associated with cancer risk (Levine et al., 2018; Ambatipudi et al., 2017; Levine et al., 2015; Dugue et al., 2021; Kresovich et al., 2019b; Kresovich et al., 2019a; Zheng et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Some studies indicate that evidence in support of the association between epigenetic age acceleration and cancer risk is weak or non existent.
source: In contrast, others indicate that evidence in support of this claim is weak or non existent (Dugué et al., 2018; Hillary et al., 2020; Durso et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Dugué et al., 2018, Hillary et al., 2020, Durso et al., 2017, and Wang et al., 2021.

claim: Positive associations between epigenetic age acceleration and colorectal cancer seem to be much stronger when biological age is estimated using second-generation clocks rather than first-generation clocks.
source: For instance, positive associations between epigenetic age acceleration and colorectal cancer seem to be much stronger when biological age is estimated using second-generation clocks (i.e. PhenoAge and GrimAge) (Dugue et al., 2021) rather than first-generation clocks (i.e. HannumAge and Intrinsic HorvathAge) (Dugué et al., 2018; Durso et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Dugue et al., 2021, Dugué et al., 2018, and Durso et al., 2017.

claim: Mendelian randomization is less likely to be affected by residual confounding and reverse causation than traditional observational methods.
source: Mendelian randomization (MR), a method that uses genetic variants as instrumental variables to infer causality between a modifiable exposure and an outcome, is less likely to be affected by residual confounding and reverse causation than traditional observational methods (Davey Smith and Ebrahim, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Davey Smith and Ebrahim, 2003.

claim: A recent genome-wide association study meta-analysis has revealed 137 genetic loci associated with epigenetic age acceleration.
source: A recent genome-wide association study (GWAS) meta-analysis has revealed 137 genetic loci associated with epigenetic age acceleration (as measured by six epigenetic biomarkers) that may be used within an MR framework (McCartney et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to McCartney et al., 2021.

claim: The GWAS meta-analysis of biological ageing included 34,710 participants of European ancestry.
source: We obtained summary genetic association estimates for epigenetic age acceleration measures of HannumAge (Hannum et al., 2013), Intrinsic HorvathAge (Horvath, 2013), PhenoAge (Levine et al., 2018), and GrimAge (Lu et al., 2019a) from a recent GWAS meta-analysis of biological ageing (McCartney et al., 2021), which included 34,710 participants of European ancestry.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text describing the data source.

claim: Across the 28 European ancestry studies considered in the analysis, 57.3% of participants were female.
source: Across the 28 European ancestry studies considered in the analysis, 57.3% of participants were female.
evidence: This is a descriptive statistic about the study population.

claim: Nine independent SNPs were identified for HannumAge acceleration.
source: We identified 9 independent SNPs for HannumAge, 24 for Intrinsic HorvathAge, 11 for PhenoAge and 4 for GrimAge (Supplementary file 1 — Table 1).
evidence: This is a result from the genetic instrument selection process.

claim: 24 independent SNPs were identified for Intrinsic HorvathAge acceleration.
source: We identified 9 independent SNPs for HannumAge, 24 for Intrinsic HorvathAge, 11 for PhenoAge and 4 for GrimAge (Supplementary file 1 — Table 1).
evidence: This is a result from the genetic instrument selection process.

claim: 11 independent SNPs were identified for PhenoAge acceleration.
source: We identified 9 independent SNPs for HannumAge, 24 for Intrinsic HorvathAge, 11 for PhenoAge and 4 for GrimAge (Supplementary file 1 — Table 1).
evidence: This is a result from the genetic instrument selection process.

claim: 4 independent SNPs were identified for GrimAge acceleration.
source: We identified 9 independent SNPs for HannumAge, 24 for Intrinsic HorvathAge, 11 for PhenoAge and 4 for GrimAge (Supplementary file 1 — Table 1).
evidence: This is a result from the genetic instrument selection process.

claim: The genetic instruments for HannumAge acceleration explained 1.48% of the trait variance.
source: The genetic instruments for HannumAge, Intrinsic HorvathAge, PhenoAge and GrimAge acceleration explained 1.48%, 4.41%, 1.86%, and 0.47% of the trait variance, respectively.
evidence: This is a calculated statistic from the genetic instrument analysis.

claim: The genetic instruments for Intrinsic HorvathAge acceleration explained 4.41% of the trait variance.
source: The genetic instruments for HannumAge, Intrinsic HorvathAge, PhenoAge and GrimAge acceleration explained 1.48%, 4.41%, 1.86%, and 0.47% of the trait variance, respectively.
evidence: This is a calculated statistic from the genetic instrument analysis.

claim: The genetic instruments for PhenoAge acceleration explained 1.86% of the trait variance.
source: The genetic instruments for HannumAge, Intrinsic HorvathAge, PhenoAge and GrimAge acceleration explained 1.48%, 4.41%, 1.86%, and 0.47% of the trait variance, respectively.
evidence: This is a calculated statistic from the genetic instrument analysis.

claim: The genetic instruments for GrimAge acceleration explained 0.47% of the trait variance.
source: The genetic instruments for HannumAge, Intrinsic HorvathAge, PhenoAge and GrimAge acceleration explained 1.48%, 4.41%, 1.86%, and 0.47% of the trait variance, respectively.
evidence: This is a calculated statistic from the genetic instrument analysis.

claim: All the selected SNPs had F-statistics greater than 10.
source: All the selected SNPs had F-statistics greater than 10 (HannumAge median 38 and range 31–99, Intrinsic HorvathAge median 47 and range 31–240, PhenoAge median 45 and range 32–89, GrimAge median 36 and range 31–45).
evidence: This is a calculated statistic demonstrating instrument strength.

claim: Meta-analysed IVW MR findings suggested that higher GrimAge acceleration increased the risk of colorectal cancer (OR = 1.12 per year increase in GrimAge acceleration, 95% CI 1.04–1.20, p = 0.002).
source: Meta-analysed IVW MR findings suggested that higher GrimAge acceleration increased the risk of colorectal cancer (OR = 1.12 per year increase in GrimAge acceleration, 95% CI 1.04–1.20, p = 0.002).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the Mendelian randomization analysis.

claim: The direction of the genetically predicted effects of GrimAge acceleration on colorectal cancer was consistent across main and sensitivity MR analyses.
source: The direction of the genetically predicted effects was consistent across main and sensitivity MR analyses.
evidence: This is an observation about the consistency of results across different analytical methods.

claim: The genetically predicted effect of GrimAge acceleration was greater for colon cancer (IVW OR = 1.15, 95% CI 1.09–1.21, p = 0.006) than rectal cancer (IVW OR = 1.05, 95% CI 0.97–1.13, p = 0.24).
source: Among subtypes, the genetically predicted effect of GrimAge acceleration was greater for colon cancer (IVW OR = 1.15, 95% CI 1.09–1.21, p = 0.006), than rectal cancer (IVW OR = 1.05, 95% CI 0.97–1.13, p = 0.24).
evidence: This is a finding from subtype-specific MR analyses.

claim: There was no strong evidence of causality between epigenetic age acceleration and breast cancer.
source: We did not find strong evidence of causality between epigenetic age acceleration and breast cancer (GrimAge IVW OR = 0.98, 95% CI 0.95–1.00, p = 0.08; PhenoAge IVW OR = 0.99, 95% CI 0.98–1.01, p = 0.23; HannumAge IVW OR = 0.99, 95% CI 0.97–1.02, p = 0.63; and Intrinsic HorvathAge IVW OR = 0.99, 95% CI 0.98–1.00, p = 0.13)
evidence: This is a finding from the MR analysis showing null results.

claim: There was limited evidence of causality between epigenetic age acceleration and ovarian cancer.
source: There was also limited evidence of causality between epigenetic age acceleration and ovarian cancer (GrimAge IVW OR = 0.99, 95% CI 0.93–1.06, p = 0.78; PhenoAge IVW OR = 0.98, 95% CI 0.96–1.01, p = 0.24; HannumAge IVW OR = 1.00, 95% CI 0.96–1.04, p = 0.95; and Intrinsic HorvathAge IVW OR = 1.00, 95% CI 0.97–1.02, p = 0.89)
evidence: This is a finding from the MR analysis showing null results.

claim: Meta-analysed IVW MR findings suggested that genetically predicted GrimAge acceleration decreased the risk of prostate cancer (OR = 0.93 per year increase in GrimAge acceleration, 95% CI 0.87–0.99, p = 0.02).
source: Meta-analysed IVW MR findings suggested that genetically predicted GrimAge acceleration decreased the risk of prostate cancer (OR = 0.93 per year increase in GrimAge acceleration, 95% CI 0.87–0.99, p = 0.02)
evidence: This is a finding from the MR analysis.

claim: The main IVW result for GrimAge and prostate cancer did not withstand multiple testing correction (FDR p = 0.16).
source: Nevertheless, these did not pass multiple testing correction. Finally, we found no consistent evidence for other measures of epigenetic age acceleration and cancers.
evidence: This is a statement about the statistical significance after correction for multiple testing.

claim: Meta-analysed IVW MR findings suggested that genetically predicted Intrinsic HorvathAge acceleration decreased the risk of lung cancer (OR = 0.97 per year increase in Intrinsic HorvathAge acceleration, 95% CI 0.93–1.00, p = 0.03).
source: Meta-analysed IVW MR findings suggested that genetically predicted Intrinsic HorvathAge acceleration decreased the risk of lung cancer (OR = 0.97 per year increase in Intrinsic HorvathAge acceleration, 95% CI 0.93–1.00, p = 0.03)
evidence: This is a finding from the MR analysis.

claim: The results for Intrinsic HorvathAge and lung cancer did not survive multiple testing correction (FDR p = 0.21).
source: However, these results did not survive multiple testing correction (FDR p = 0.21)
evidence: This is a statement about the statistical significance after correction for multiple testing.

claim: The GrimAge and colorectal cancer results survived multiple testing correction (FDR p = 0.04).
source: These results survived multiple testing correction (FDR p = 0.04)
evidence: This is a statement about the statistical significance after correction for multiple testing.

claim: There was little evidence of heterogeneity across FinnGen and GECCO estimates for GrimAge and colorectal cancer (I2 = 0%, 95% CI 'NA', p = 0.61).
source: These results survived multiple testing correction (FDR p = 0.04) and there was little evidence of heterogeneity across FinnGen and GECCO estimates (I2 = 0%, 95% CI 'NA', p = 0.61).
evidence: This is a statistical measure of heterogeneity across studies.

claim: Results for GrimAge and colorectal cancer were consistent when using UK Biobank data alone (IVW OR = 1.15, 95% CI 1.04–1.28, p = 0.007).
source: and results were consistent when using UK Biobank data alone (IVW OR = 1.15, 95% CI 1.04–1.28, p = 0.007)
evidence: This is a finding from a sensitivity analysis using a single data source.

claim: There was no evidence of residual population stratification in MR analyses using negative control outcomes.
source: We did not find evidence of residual population stratification in MR analyses using negative control outcomes (Appendix 2—figure 9, Supplementary file 1 — Table s7)
evidence: This is a finding from a sensitivity analysis using negative controls.

claim: There was no evidence of horizontal pleiotropy via potential colorectal cancer risk factors.
source: nor did we find evidence of horizontal pleiotropy via potential colorectal cancer risk factors (Appendix 2—figure 10, Supplementary file 1 — Table s8).
evidence: This is a finding from a sensitivity analysis examining potential pleiotropic pathways.

claim: Single-SNP analysis revealed that the effect of GrimAge on colorectal cancer was not driven by a single SNP.
source: Single-SNP analysis revealed that the effect was not driven by a single SNP (Supplementary file 1 — Table s9).
evidence: This is a finding from a sensitivity analysis examining individual SNP contributions.

claim: There was no detectable evidence of uncorrelated horizontal pleiotropy for GrimAge and colorectal cancer (MR-Egger intercept = –0.13, 95% CI –0.33–0.07, p = 0.33).
source: Moreover, there was no detectable evidence of uncorrelated horizontal pleiotropy (MR-Egger intercept = –0.13, 95% CI –0.33–0.07, p = 0.33)
evidence: This is a finding from the MR-Egger intercept test.

claim: There was no heterogeneity across individual SNP estimates for GrimAge and colorectal cancer (Cochran's Q 7.12, p = 0.07).
source: or heterogeneity across individual SNP estimates (Cochran's Q 7.12, p = 0.07)
evidence: This is a finding from Cochran's Q test for heterogeneity.

claim: CAUSE analyses found no evidence against bias due to correlated pleiotropy for GrimAge and colorectal cancer (CAUSE OR = 1.00, 95% credible intervals 0.96–1.04, p = 1.00; shared q = 4%, 95% credible intervals 0–24%).
source: We further explored the genetically predicted effect of GrimAge on colorectal cancer using GECCO data only and found no evidence against bias due to correlated pleiotropy (CAUSE OR = 1.00, 95% credible intervals 0.96–1.04, p = 1.00; shared q = 4%, 95% credible intervals 0–24%)
evidence: This is a finding from the CAUSE analysis.

claim: Strong evidence was found for a causal relationship between GrimAge acceleration and colon cancer (IVW OR = 1.15, 95% CI 1.09–1.21, p = 0.006).
source: Among subtypes, we found strong evidence for a causal relationship between GrimAge acceleration and colon cancer (IVW OR = 1.15, 95% CI 1.09–1.21, p = 0.006).
evidence: This is a finding from subtype-specific MR analysis.

claim: No evidence was found for a causal relationship between GrimAge acceleration and rectal cancer (IVW OR = 1.05, 95% CI 0.97–1.13, p = 0.24).
source: In contrast, we did not find such evidence for rectal cancer (IVW OR = 1.05, 95% CI 0.97–1.13, p = 0.24).
evidence: This is a finding from subtype-specific MR analysis.

claim: The magnitude of the genetically predicted effect of GrimAge acceleration on colon cancer was the same for distal (IVW OR = 1.16, 95% CI 1.03–1.29, p = 0.01) and proximal colon cancer (IVW OR = 1.16, 95% CI 0.97–1.40, p = 0.11).
source: After further stratification, the magnitude of the genetically predicted effect of GrimAge acceleration on colon cancer was the same for distal (IVW OR = 1.16, 95% CI 1.03–1.29, p = 0.01) and proximal colon cancer (IVW OR = 1.16, 95% CI 0.97–1.40, p = 0.11).
evidence: This is a finding from further subtype-specific MR analysis.

claim: Sex-stratified results suggest that GrimAge acceleration may influence colorectal cancer in both males (IVW OR = 1.12, 95% CI 1.00–1.25, p = 0.05) and females (IVW OR = 1.14, 95% CI 1.04–1.26, p = 0.008).
source: Also, sex-stratified results suggest that GrimAge acceleration may influence colorectal cancer in both males (IVW OR = 1.12, 95% CI 1.00–1.25, p = 0.05) and females (IVW OR = 1.14, 95% CI 1.04–1.26, p = 0.008)
evidence: This is a finding from sex-stratified MR analysis.

claim: There was a positive association between GrimAge acceleration and parental history of colorectal cancer (OR = 1.06, 95% CI 1.00–1.12, p = 0.03).
source: These findings were further supported by evidence of a positive association between GrimAge acceleration and parental history of colorectal cancer (OR = 1.06, 95% CI 1.00–1.12, p = 0.03)
evidence: This is a finding from MR analysis using parental history data.

claim: LD Score regression coefficients for GrimAge acceleration and colorectal cancer were in the expected direction (GECCO rg = 0.28, p < 0.001; UK Biobank rg = 0.15, p = 0.21; FinnGen rg = 0.27, p = 0.29).
source: Additionally, LD Score regression coefficients for GrimAge acceleration and colorectal cancer were also in the expected direction (GECCO rg = 0.28, p < 0.001; UK Biobank rg = 0.15, p = 0.21; FinnGen rg = 0.27, p = 0.29)
evidence: This is a finding from LD Score regression analysis.

claim: Evidence was found that genetically predicted GrimAge acceleration may be a cause of telomere shortening (IVW beta coefficient = −0.07 per year increase in GrimAge acceleration, 95% CI –0.09 to –0.05, p < 0.001).
source: In bidirectional MR analyses, we found evidence that genetically predicted GrimAge acceleration may be a cause of telomere shortening (IVW beta coefficient = −0.07 per year increase in GrimAge acceleration, 95% CI –0.09 to –0.05, p < 0.001)
evidence: This is a finding from bidirectional MR analysis.

claim: Evidence was found that genetically predicted longer telomere length may increase Intrinsic HorvathAge acceleration (IVW beta coefficient = 0.57 per standard deviation increase in telomere length, 95% CI 0.39–0.77, p = 0.002).
source: and that genetically predicted longer telomere length may increase Intrinsic HorvathAge acceleration (IVW beta coefficient = 0.57 per standard deviation increase in telomere length, 95% CI 0.39–0.77, p = 0.002)
evidence: This is a finding from bidirectional MR analysis.

claim: The MR estimates for the association between GrimAge and colorectal cancer were consistent with those reported in an observational nested case-control study in the Melbourne Collaborative Cohort Study (RR = 1.04 per year increase in GrimAge acceleration, 95% CI 1.01–1.07, p = 0.02).
source: Our MR estimates for the association between GrimAge and colorectal cancer were consistent with those reported in Dugue et al., 2021, an observational nested case-control study in the Melbourne Collaborative Cohort Study (RR = 1.04 per year increase in GrimAge acceleration, 95% CI 1.01–1.07, p = 0.02).
evidence: This is a comparison with findings from a cited observational study.

claim: The findings contrast with those highlighted in Hillary et al., 2020, an observational cohort study that used Generation Scotland data, which observed no evidence of an association between GrimAge acceleration and colorectal cancer after correcting for multiple testing.
source: However, our findings contrast with those highlighted in Hillary et al., 2020, an observational cohort study that used Generation Scotland data. The latter authors observed no evidence of an association between GrimAge acceleration and colorectal cancer after correcting for multiple testing.
evidence: This is a comparison with findings from a cited observational study.

claim: GrimAge may plausibly influence cancer risk through hormonal, inflammatory and metabolic processes.
source: Although little is known about the underlying mechanisms, GrimAge may plausibly influence cancer risk through hormonal, inflammatory and metabolic processes (Yu et al., 2020; Bottazzi et al., 2018; Lau and Robinson, 2021).
evidence: This is a speculative claim about potential mechanisms, supported by citations.

claim: Shorter telomeres have been shown to lower cancer risk in prior MR analyses.
source: Shorter telomeres have been shown to lower cancer risk in prior MR analyses (Telomeres Mendelian Randomization Collaboration et al., 2017; Gao et al., 2020; Kuo et al., 2019)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior MR studies.

claim: It is plausible that GrimAge acceleration decreases cancer risk, at least in part, via its effect on telomere length.
source: so it is plausible that GrimAge acceleration decreases cancer risk, at least in part, via its effect on telomere length.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the bidirectional MR findings and prior literature.

claim: GrimAge acceleration may still increase cancer risk via pathways other than those related to cellular division.
source: GrimAge acceleration may still increase cancer risk via pathways other than those related to cellular division.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential alternative mechanisms.

claim: The positive effect of GrimAge acceleration on cancer via other pathways may counteract the negative effects mediated via telomere length, resulting in null MR results for GrimAge acceleration and breast, ovarian, prostate and lung cancer, and positive MR results for GrimAge acceleration and colorectal cancer.
source: The positive effect of GrimAge acceleration on cancer via these other pathways may counteract the negative effects mediated via telomere length, resulting in null MR results for GrimAge acceleration and breast, ovarian, prostate and lung cancer, and positive MR results for GrimAge acceleration and colorectal cancer.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the pattern of results observed.

claim: The study only identified four genetic instruments for GrimAge acceleration, which explained 0.47% of the variance in the trait.
source: We only identified four genetic instruments for GrimAge acceleration, which explained 0.47% of the variance in the trait.
evidence: This is a limitation acknowledged by the authors based on their data.

claim: The GrimAge analyses were underpowered to detect ORs < 1.20 for colorectal cancer.
source: First, our GrimAge analyses were underpowered to detect ORs < 1.20 for colorectal cancer.
evidence: This is a statement about statistical power based on the study design.

claim: The study was underpowered to detect genetically predicted effects of GrimAge acceleration on cancer subtypes and cancers with smaller sample sizes.
source: Similarly, our study was underpowered to detect genetically predicted effects of GrimAge acceleration on cancer subtypes and cancers with smaller sample sizes (i.e. ovarian and lung cancer).
evidence: This is a statement about statistical power based on the study design.

claim: Different epigenetic clocks may capture information on distinct underlying biological ageing mechanisms.
source: Different clocks may capture information on distinct underlying biological ageing mechanisms (Liu et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Liu et al., 2020.

claim: GrimAge was trained on mortality and smoking, factors which are closely related to cancer risk.
source: For example, GrimAge was trained on mortality and smoking (factors which are closely related to cancer risk), which may explain why it outperforms other measures of epigenetic ageing in predicting time-to-cancer (Lu et al., 2019a).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lu et al., 2019a.

claim: GrimAge outperforms other measures of epigenetic ageing in predicting time-to-cancer.
source: For example, GrimAge was trained on mortality and smoking (factors which are closely related to cancer risk), which may explain why it outperforms other measures of epigenetic ageing in predicting time-to-cancer (Lu et al., 2019a).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lu et al., 2019a.

claim: DNAm telomere length is independent of telomerase activity.
source: To better understand the biology of ageing, future studies should consider running MR analyses using data on DNAm-predicted telomere length, since DNAm telomere length is independent of telomerase activity and has been more strongly associated with age than measured telomere length (Lu et al., 2019b).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lu et al., 2019b.

claim: DNAm telomere length has been more strongly associated with age than measured telomere length.
source: To better understand the biology of ageing, future studies should consider running MR analyses using data on DNAm-predicted telomere length, since DNAm telomere length is independent of telomerase activity and has been more strongly associated with age than measured telomere length (Lu et al., 2019b).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lu et al., 2019b.

claim: Observational and Mendelian randomization studies suggest that GrimAge acceleration may be influenced by several cancer risk factors, such as obesity and smoking.
source: Observational and Mendelian randomization studies suggest that GrimAge acceleration may be influenced by several cancer risk factors, such as obesity and smoking (Lu et al., 2019a; McCartney et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Lu et al., 2019a and McCartney et al., 2021.

claim: The selection of 'super controls' could have inflated cancer GWAS effect sizes and MR estimates.
source: The selection of 'super controls' (e.g. in UK Biobank, FinnGen and GECCO), with no other cancers, related lesions (i.e. benign, in situ, uncertain or unspecified behaviour neoplasms) or reported family history of cancer, could have inflated cancer GWAS effect sizes (and our MR estimates), because 'super controls' are healthier than the general population and are less likely to be genetically predisposed to develop cancer.
evidence: This is a limitation acknowledged by the authors based on inference about the study design.

claim: It is unlikely that the genetic architecture of epigenetic clock acceleration differs across sexes, as DNAm levels at individual clock CpGs are highly correlated between males and females.
source: However, it is unlikely that the genetic architecture of epigenetic clock acceleration differs across sexes, as DNAm levels at individual clock CpGs are highly correlated between males and females (Grodstein et al., 2020; Tajuddin et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Grodstein et al., 2020 and Tajuddin et al., 2019.

claim: The study was conducted using data from participants of European ancestry only to reduce bias due to population stratification.
source: Finally, to reduce bias due to population stratification, this study was conducted using data from participants of European ancestry only.
evidence: This is a description of the study design choice.

claim: The GWAS data used for the analyses had been adjusted for the top genetic principal components to reduce bias due to population stratification.
source: The GWAS data used for the analyses had been adjusted for the top genetic principal components for the same reason.
evidence: This is a description of the data processing methods.

claim: MR of negative control outcomes suggests that the MR results are unlikely to be biased by residual population stratification.
source: Furthermore, our MR of negative control outcomes suggests that our MR results are unlikely to be biased by residual population stratification.
evidence: This is an inference based on the results of the negative control analysis.

claim: Confounding due to population stratification, dynastic effects and assortative mating cannot be ruled out completely.
source: Despite this, confounding due to population stratification, dynastic effects and assortative mating cannot be ruled out completely, as it is not possible to test the second MR assumption (i.e. independence assumption).
evidence: This is a limitation acknowledged by the authors based on the inherent limitations of MR.

claim: Family history data correlate with combined hospital record and questionnaire data and provide better power to detect GWAS-significant associations for some phenotypes in the UK Biobank.
source: Family history data correlate with combined hospital record and questionnaire data and it has been suggested that they provide better power to detect GWAS-significant associations for some phenotypes in the UK Biobank (DeBoever et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to DeBoever et al., 2020.

claim: Steiger filtering showed that all genetic instruments for GrimAge acceleration were stronger predictors of GrimAge acceleration than telomere length.
source: Steiger filtering showed that all genetic instruments for GrimAge acceleration were stronger predictors of GrimAge acceleration than telomere length.
evidence: This is a finding from the Steiger directionality test.

claim: Steiger filtering identified 20 genetic instruments for telomere length that were better predictors of Intrinsic HorvathAge acceleration than telomere length.
source: In contrast, it identified 20 genetic instruments for telomere length that were better predictors of Intrinsic HorvathAge acceleration than telomere length (Supplementary file 1 — Table s15).
evidence: This is a finding from the Steiger directionality test.

claim: After removing SNPs identified by Steiger filtering, the results were still suggestive of an effect of telomere length on Intrinsic HorvathAge acceleration (IVW beta coefficient = 0.71 per standard deviation increase in telomere length, 95% CI 0.57–0.85, p < 0.001).
source: After removing these SNPs from the analyses, the results were still suggestive of an effect of telomere length on Intrinsic HorvathAge acceleration (IVW beta coefficient = 0.71 per standard deviation increase in telomere length, 95% CI 0.57–0.85, p < 0.001)
evidence: This is a finding from a sensitivity analysis after Steiger filtering.

claim: There was little evidence of causality between other measures of epigenetic age acceleration and telomere length.
source: There was little evidence of causality between other measures of epigenetic age acceleration and telomere length (Appendix 2—figure 13, Supplementary file 1 — Table s14).
evidence: This is a finding from the bidirectional MR analysis.

claim: The study had 80% power to detect ORs as small as 1.04–1.39 across combinations of the four epigenetic clock acceleration and five cancer measures.
